analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone can buy, alongside stronger ACA subsidies and a Medicare out-of-pocket cap.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Senator Merkley and 12 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would create a new government-run health plan, 'Medicare Part E,' that any resident could buy on the ACA exchanges and that employers could voluntarily offer to workers instead of private insurance. It would cover gold-level benefits including reproductive care nationwide, cap Medicare beneficiaries' yearly out-of-pocket costs at $6,700, make ACA subsidies more generous and available above 400% of the poverty line, boost cost-sharing help for lower-income enrollees, and put $30 billion into a reinsurance fund to lower individual-market premiums. The plan would pay doctors and hospitals rates negotiated between current Medicare rates and the average commercial rates, and it would apply Medicare's drug-price negotiation rules to its prescriptions.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and individually insured people gain a government-run plan option that covers more (gold level, reproductive services regardless of state bans) and cannot balance-bill. Lower- and middle-income exchange enrollees get bigger subsidies pegged to gold plans rather than silver, plus richer cost-sharing reductions. Medicare beneficiaries get a hard $6,700 annual out-of-pocket cap. Workers whose employer coverage is unaffordable get a legal right to be referred to exchange navigators, and workers on a Part E employer plan keep their coverage if they lose their job.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured people, exchange enrollees, Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans open to any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP, offered in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets through the exchanges. [S2]

Part E plans must cover all Medicare-covered benefits plus essential health benefits at gold level, must cover abortions and all other reproductive services, and states are barred from banning that coverage. [S2]

The plan must pay providers rates negotiated between Medicare rates and the average rates commercial exchange plans pay, applies Medicare's balance-billing limits to participating providers, and extends Medicare's prescription drug negotiation provisions to the new plan. [S2]
Starting in 2026, Medicare beneficiaries' total annual cost-sharing for Part A and B services is capped at $6,700, adjusted for medical inflation. [S2]

ACA premium subsidies would be calculated against the second-lowest-cost gold plan rather than silver, eligibility would be made permanent above the 400% poverty line, and cost-sharing reductions would be increased so lower-income enrollees get plans covering up to 94% of costs. [S2]

$30 billion is appropriated for state reinsurance or affordability programs for 2025-2027 to reduce individual-market premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and $2 billion funds startup of the public plan. [S2]

Employers that do not offer affordable, adequate coverage must refer full-time employees to exchange navigators, and workers on a Part E employer plan can keep that coverage after losing their job. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers lose customers and market share to a government-run competitor in every market. Hospitals and doctors face payment rates below commercial averages for Part E patients and Medicare's balance-billing prohibition. Taxpayers fund the $2 billion startup appropriation and the $30 billion reinsurance and affordability fund. In the large-group market, extending community rating could raise premiums for younger, healthier groups to subsidize older, sicker ones.

drawbacks.text: Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's benefit and administrative costs, so unless the government plan's lower payments translate into lower premiums, it may not be dramatically cheaper than private options for individuals. [S2]

Paying providers between Medicare and commercial rates and banning balance billing could lead some hospitals and doctors to limit participation, which the bill tries to manage through network-adequacy requirements rather than guarantee. [S2]

Extending community rating to the large-group market and boosting subsidies and reinsurance involves real federal spending ($30 billion over three years, plus startup funds and reserve appropriations), and some of the reinsurance money flows directly to private insurers. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefits are substantial and concrete: a public plan option with broad coverage and no balance billing, larger ACA subsidies, a Medicare out-of-pocket cap, and $30 billion to reduce premiums and cost-sharing. The main trade-offs are the federal cost of the subsidies and reinsurance, uncertainty about whether the self-financing public plan can hold premiums down enough to compete, and possible provider-network friction. The design is standard for a public-option proposal rather than a single-payer plan, so the private insurance industry keeps most of the market; the public plan competes with it rather than replacing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 1, 2024, sent to the Senate Finance Committee that same day, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2024, with 12 Democratic cosponsors. [S1]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced. [S4]
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee held no markup and the Senate never debated or voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers are better off: no competing public plan was created in their markets, Medicare's drug negotiation powers were not extended to it, and the rate and balance-billing constraints on providers never took effect. Medicare beneficiaries also continue to face uncapped Part A/B cost-sharing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and their market position

industries.note: A government-run Medicare Part E plan would compete for customers in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, and Medicare's drug negotiation and balance-billing rules would extend to it. The industry's loss of market share is the public's gain in the form of a cheaper, more comprehensive option; the bill's $30 billion reinsurance fund, however, would partly offset insurer losses in the individual market.

Part E would pay providers at negotiated rates no lower than Medicare but no higher than the average commercial exchange rates, below what private plans typically pay, and would extend Medicare's balance-billing ban. Providers also gain a guaranteed pool of participating providers and new customers, which is why the effect is not purely negative.
The bill applies Medicare's drug-price negotiation provisions and the related excise tax to drugs covered by Part E plans, extending the negotiation regime to a new block of covered lives.
Employers could voluntarily offer a public plan option in the group market or use the government as a third-party administrator, giving them a new, standardized alternative to private carriers.
